title: {{NAME}} and the Clockwork Meadow of Wonders
moral: The most extraordinary magic comes not from spells or circuits, but from the courage to reach out a hand in friendship.

pages.content:
Beyond the last house on Willowmere Lane, past the ancient oak whose roots curled like sleeping dragons, lay the Clockwork Meadow. Nobody from town had ever walked its shimmering border — not really, not all the way in. But {{NAME}} had always wondered about the soft blue glow that pulsed there each evening, steady as a heartbeat.

The meadow stretched enormous and wild beneath a violet sky. Brass sunflowers the height of lampposts swayed in a breeze that smelled of honeysuckle and machine oil. Tiny fairy lights bobbed between their stems, and at the very centre stood something that made {{NAME}}'s breath catch like a kite in a tree.

It was a robot, easily three times as tall as any grown-up, built from polished copper and hammered silver. Its chest glowed with a warm amber lantern, its enormous hands were folded gently in its lap, and from every joint and hinge tiny wildflowers had grown, looping green stems through the bolts as though nature and machine had decided, quietly, to become friends.

Beside the robot stood a unicorn. Her coat was the colour of fresh snow at dusk, faintly lavender, and her mane cascaded like ribbons of moonlight. She watched {{NAME}} with eyes that were ancient and calm and entirely unafraid.

pages.content:
A tiny voice rang out like a silver bell dropped on a marble floor. 'You came! You actually came!'

{{NAME}} spun around. Hovering at perfect nose-height was the smallest, most luminous fairy he had ever imagined. She had wings like stained glass, flushed with copper and emerald, and her dress appeared to be stitched entirely from shed unicorn hairs, each one catching the light differently. Her name, she announced with tremendous dignity, was Pip.

'Pip,' {{NAME}} repeated, and couldn't help grinning.

'Don't laugh at my name,' she said, though she was smiling too. 'I have been watching you peer at this meadow for three whole weeks. You always stop at the oak. You always look, and then you walk away.' She crossed her tiny arms. 'What changed tonight?'

{{NAME}} thought about it honestly. He had been nervous, obviously, and the meadow was strange and unknown, and his heart had always said wait. But tonight, for no particular reason he could name, his feet had simply kept walking.

'I decided the wondering was worse than the not-knowing,' he said.

Pip's wings blazed brilliant gold. 'Oh,' she breathed, 'that is exactly the right answer. Come on, then. Cogsworth won't bite. He's never bitten anyone. He doesn't even have proper teeth.'

pages.content:
Cogsworth, it turned out, was magnificent.

The great copper robot could do things that made {{NAME}}'s brain fizz with joy. When Pip sang a single note, Cogsworth would tilt his enormous domed head and replicate the sound from somewhere deep in his chest cavity, only warmer, richer, like the note had been wrapped in velvet. He could juggle the brass sunflowers, tossing three at a time with the delicate precision of a watchmaker. Most astonishing of all, he could project constellations from the lantern in his chest, scattering tiny stars across the meadow grass.

The unicorn, whose name was Seraphel, danced through the projected starlight. Her hooves never quite touched the ground properly when she moved like this, as if gravity were merely a suggestion she entertained politely.

'She's been trying to reach the highest star for months,' Pip confided, perching on {{NAME}}'s shoulder. 'The one that spins at the top of Cogsworth's projection. She says it smells like adventure.'

{{NAME}} looked at Seraphel leaping, at Cogsworth raising his projection higher and higher to help her, at Pip's tiny face pulled into fierce concentration. None of them had asked for anything. They had simply shared their world.

He kicked off his amber boots, feeling the cool meadow grass under his feet, and ran headlong into the cascade of stars alongside Seraphel, laughing so loudly that actual fireflies came to investigate.

pages.content:
Then Cogsworth went still.

Not sleepily still, not resting-still. Completely, terribly still. The lantern in his chest flickered twice, dimmed to a faint ember, and the stars all vanished at once.

Seraphel stopped mid-leap and landed heavily. Pip made no sound at all, which was, {{NAME}} had learned in roughly twenty minutes, the most frightening thing she could do.

'His core crystal,' Pip whispered finally. 'It's cracking. It cracks a little more every month. One day it will shatter entirely and he will simply... stop.'

{{NAME}} looked up at Cogsworth's face. The amber glow had nearly gone. The wildflowers growing from his joints had drooped, their green stems gone pale. He looked smaller somehow, though nothing about him had changed in size.

Seraphel stepped forward and pressed her spiralled horn very gently against Cogsworth's chest, right where the lantern pulsed its last weak light. Her own glow intensified, flowing silver and gold down the length of her horn and into the copper casing. Cogsworth shuddered. The lantern flickered. The wildflowers straightened.

'She does this every time,' Pip said softly. 'She gives him some of her own light.'

{{NAME}} reached out without thinking and placed both his hands flat against the warm copper plating beside Seraphel's horn. He had no magic, no horn, no wings. But his hands were warm, and he pressed them there with everything he had.

pages.content:
The lantern blazed back to life. Brighter than before. Brighter than Pip had ever seen it, she said, and she said it three times to make sure everyone understood.

Cogsworth's head swivelled down slowly. His enormous amber eyes, two curved plates of polished glass, focused on {{NAME}} with a warmth that had nothing mechanical about it. He reached down with one careful copper finger and, very gently, tucked a single brass buttercup behind {{NAME}}'s ear.

Seraphel nuzzled {{NAME}}'s shoulder, leaving a faint shimmer of silver on his teal jacket. Pip sat on his head and refused to move for a considerable time.

Eventually the violet sky deepened to indigo, and the first real stars appeared, distant and quiet above the brass sunflowers. {{NAME}} put his amber boots back on, one at a time, slowly, because he did not especially want to leave.

'Will you come back?' Pip asked from her spot in his hair.

'Tomorrow,' {{NAME}} said. Not maybe. Not I'll try. Tomorrow.

He walked home through the meadow's blue glow, the brass buttercup still tucked behind his ear, already warm from the goodnight that waited at home, and already wondering what he would discover the next time Cogsworth's chest lit up the violet sky.

Because Pip had mentioned, very quietly just before he left, that the highest spinning star? It had moved. Just slightly. Just enough.
